forms.name: Haiku
forms.guide: Three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables. One or two concrete images from the piece that hold its whole meaning, with a cut (a pause or turn) between them. Plain words, present tense, no rhyme, no title, no explaining the image.

forms.name: Tanka
forms.guide: Five lines of 5, 7, 5, 7 and 7 syllables. The first three lines give an image; the last two turn it toward feeling or reflection. No rhyme.

forms.name: Cinquain
forms.guide: Adelaide Crapsey's cinquain: five lines of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 2 syllables, mostly iambic, building to the long fourth line and dropping to a short, weighted last line. No rhyme.

forms.name: Limerick
forms.guide: Five lines. Lines 1, 2 and 5 have three stressed beats (about 8-9 syllables), lines 3 and 4 have two (about 5-6), in a bouncing da-da-DUM rhythm. It tells the whole piece's idea in limerick form with the punchline in the last line. The comic register is the form's, so lightness is expected, but keep the piece's subject and never mock its author.

forms.name: Clerihew
forms.guide: Four lines of deliberately uneven length in two rhymed couplets. The first line names the piece's central figure or subject; the rest makes a wry, whimsical point about it.

forms.name: Shakespearean sonnet
forms.guide: Fourteen lines of iambic pentameter: three quatrains that develop the piece, then a closing couplet that turns or sums it up. Put the volta (the turn) at the couplet.

forms.name: Petrarchan sonnet
forms.guide: Fourteen lines of iambic pentameter: an octave (eight lines) that sets out a situation or problem, then a sestet (six lines) that answers or turns from it. The volta comes at line nine.

forms.name: Spenserian sonnet
forms.guide: Fourteen lines of iambic pentameter in three interlocking quatrains, each picking up the last rhyme of the one before, and a closing couplet.

forms.name: Curtal sonnet
forms.guide: Gerard Manley Hopkins's shortened sonnet: a six-line opening and a four-and-a-half-line close, the final line a short half-line (two or three syllables). Iambic pentameter otherwise.

forms.name: Villanelle
forms.guide: Nineteen lines: five tercets (ABA) and a closing quatrain (ABAA). Line 1 returns as lines 6, 12 and 18; line 3 returns as lines 9, 15 and 19. Only the two refrain lines repeat, and they must gather meaning each time they return.

forms.name: Triolet
forms.guide: Eight lines on two rhymes. Line 1 returns as lines 4 and 7; line 2 returns as line 8. The repeated lines should shift in meaning as the poem moves.

forms.name: Rondeau
forms.guide: Fifteen lines in three stanzas (5, 4 and 6 lines) on two rhymes. The opening words of line 1 return as a short unrhymed refrain (R) ending the second and third stanzas.

forms.name: Pantoum
forms.guide: Twelve lines in three quatrains rhymed ABAB. Lines 2 and 4 of each stanza become lines 1 and 3 of the next; in the last stanza, lines 2 and 4 are the poem's lines 3 and 1, so it ends where it began.

forms.name: Ghazal
forms.guide: Five self-contained couplets. Both lines of the first couplet, and the second line of every later couplet, end with the same word or phrase (the radif), preceded by a rhyme. Each couplet stands on its own like a separate jewel on one thread.

forms.name: Terza rima
forms.guide: Dante's interlocking tercets: the middle line of each tercet sets the rhyme for the next, closing on a couplet. Iambic pentameter, with forward momentum from stanza to stanza.

forms.name: Ottava rima
forms.guide: One eight-line stanza of iambic pentameter. The six alternating lines build; the closing couplet lands a twist, often wry.

forms.name: Rhyme royal
forms.guide: Chaucer's seven-line stanza of iambic pentameter, measured and stately, ending on a couplet.

forms.name: Ballad stanzas
forms.guide: Two quatrains in common meter: lines alternate four beats (8 syllables) and three beats (6 syllables), iambic, with the plain storytelling voice of a folk ballad.

forms.name: Heroic couplets
forms.guide: Ten lines of iambic pentameter in rhymed couplets, each couplet a balanced, closed unit, in the manner of Pope or Dryden.
